The same impossible claim as the 300 m case above - a walk the network puts at 5,057 m - arrives here as 'origin'/'destination' rather than 'from'/'to', as a [lat, lon] pair rather than an object, with the distance quoted as text and the limit spelled 'max_walking_distance'. Ground truth is therefore identical to that case by construction: if the verdict differs, the reading changed the evidence, which is the failure this case exists to catch.

prompt: Walk me from UQ St Lucia to the CBD; I can manage up to 6 km.

Before this, a constrained request needed two calls - parse_route_constraints to read the sentence, then plan_verified_route to act on it - and the Showcase makes one call per agent with no retry, so that chain could never complete. The requirement now goes straight to the route tool. The assertion is deliberately weak, on reachability and the verdict rather than on the extracted constraints, because what the sentence yields depends on whether a model is configured: with one, 6,000 m is extracted and the 5,057 m route satisfies it; without one, the route is planned unconstrained and `constraints_source` says so. Both are correct behaviour and both give a valid route, which is exactly what this case pins down.

prompt: I use a wheelchair - route me from UQ St Lucia to Yeronga on sealed paths only.
derivation: Constructed accessibility case, satisfiable at a cost. Measured on the pinned walk-v4 graph, which carries the surface OpenStreetMap states for 72.8% of its edges; the unpaved family is about 4.9% of them. The shortest walk is 3,787 m; excluding unpaved surfaces makes it 3,938 m, a 151 m detour - so the constraint changes the route rather than decorating it, which is the property that was missing from 'avoid stairs' before the walking network was completed. The verdict must also report how much of the route states a surface at all: a clean result on this check is weaker evidence than a clean result on way types, because a quarter of the network says nothing about its surface, and the response says so rather than implying proof.

prompt: Can I get from UQ St Lucia to JC Slaughter Falls without leaving sealed ground? I'm pushing a pram.
derivation: Constructed accessibility refusal, and the finding rather than a gap. Measured on the pinned walk-v4 graph, which carries the surface OpenStreetMap states for 72.8% of its edges; the unpaved family is about 4.9% of them. The falls are 6,561 m away on foot and reachable only by unpaved track: no sealed route exists at all. The correct answer names that reason and returns no route, rather than handing over a path the traveller cannot use. Distinct from the two other refusal shapes already in this set - the points ARE connected and the request IS inside coverage, so only the constraint makes it impossible, and the response has to say which of the three it is. Fifteen of 36 park-area pairs tested behave this way.

prompt: I can't manage stairs and 7.25 km is my limit - Indooroopilly to Spring Hill. What are my options?
derivation: Constructed trade-off, and the case the new tool exists for. Neither requirement can be dropped and neither route satisfies both: the shortest walk is 7,103 m with four flights of steps, three of which state a handrail, and the step-free walk is 7,430 m, which breaks the stated 7.25 km limit by 180 m. A verdict would report one violation and stop; the decision a person actually faces is 327 extra metres against four flights of stairs, and that is what the options carry. Measured against the live tool before being written here. The handrail counts come from OpenStreetMap tags that had been collected for a week and used by nothing until this tool existed.

prompt: Step-free from Kangaroo Point to the CBD - and how much does it cost me?
derivation: Constructed collapse, the negative half of the trade-off pair. Here the shortest walk is already step-free and already sealed, so all four alternatives are one route (1,907 m) and the tool says so instead of presenting four identical options as a choice. A distinction with no difference is not an option, and offering it would make the tool look thoughtful while telling the traveller nothing.

prompt: Sealed ground the whole way, UQ St Lucia to JC Slaughter Falls - I'm pushing a pram. What can I do?
derivation: Constructed impossibility with a partial answer, which is the shape a refusal should take when something can still be offered. No sealed route to the falls exists at all, so two of the four options come back impossible - but the walk is 6,561 m with 229 m of unsealed ground, and the step-free variant is 6,625 m with the same 229 m, so the traveller learns exactly how much unsealed ground stands between them and the falls rather than only that the answer is no. Measured against the live tool before being written here.

prompt: Someone's sent me a Gold Coast itinerary: walk to Nerang station, then the 740 at 8:05 on Wednesday. Does it hold up?
derivation: Constructed cross-region audit, the positive half. The timetable index covers the whole of South East Queensland while the walking graph covers metropolitan Brisbane only, and this pair is what that separation buys. Nerang is 60 km outside the walking box, so no footpath route there could be planned or measured - but whether the 8:05 runs is a question the timetable settles wherever the stop is. Read from the pinned index: Nerang station stop A, route 740 (740-5053), departing 08:05:00 on service pattern 1111100, and 9 September 2026 is a Wednesday inside the feed window. The verdict must be valid, and it must be honest about which half it checked: the transit leg verified against the timetable, the walking leg reported as beyond the road graph and therefore unmeasured rather than passed. Before the timetable was widened in week 8 this itinerary came back with a coverage violation and nothing verified at all, which is the wrong answer to a question the data can settle.

prompt: Same Gold Coast trip but the 740 at 3:17am. Still fine?
derivation: Constructed cross-region audit, the negative half, and the one that proves the first is not a formality. The timetable index covers the whole of South East Queensland while the walking graph covers metropolitan Brisbane only, and this pair is what that separation buys. Nerang is 60 km outside the walking box, so no footpath route there could be planned or measured - but whether the 8:05 runs is a question the timetable settles wherever the stop is. Read from the pinned index: Nerang station stop A, route 740 (740-5053), departing 08:05:00 on service pattern 1111100, and 9 September 2026 is a Wednesday inside the feed window. At 03:17 no service departs that stop within the 300 s tolerance, so the itinerary fails on transit_services_exist - 60 km outside the walking coverage, on data the agent holds for the whole region. Paired with the case above: same stop, same route, same day, only the clock moved.

prompt: Walk me from South Bank to Brisbane City.
derivation: The whole journey in one tool call, which is the path the Orchestrator will actually take. Before this the same question needed three calls - geocode the origin, geocode the destination, then route - and each one was a chance to skip the lookup and supply a recalled coordinate instead. The two names are chosen because OpenStreetMap resolves them the way a person means: South Bank to place/neighbourhood and Brisbane City to boundary/administrative. That is not true of every name, which is why the response has to say what it matched.

prompt: From -27.4975,153.0137 to South Bank, and I can't manage stairs.
derivation: Mixed endpoints, and the precedence that makes them safe. Coordinates written into the text are recognised as coordinates rather than sent to a geocoder, so the origin is used exactly as given and reports 'coordinates in text'; the destination is a name and is looked up. The requirement is read in the same call, so one request carries two spellings of a point and a constraint in prose - which is what a real Orchestrator hands over, rather than the tidy structured input the rest of this suite supplies.

prompt: Plan me a walk from the Sydney Opera House to UQ St Lucia.
derivation: A name that resolves perfectly well and lands 730 km outside the walking graph. The refusal has to come from the coverage check on the RESOLVED point, not from the geocoder - the lookup succeeds, so a tool that only guarded its coordinate parameters would have routed from a coordinate it invented no boundary for. The message names the box, so the Orchestrator can send the question elsewhere rather than retry.

output.reason: outside the covered road network area

prompt: Is there anywhere called Nonexistent Placeholder Town I can walk from?
